UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine submits this Memorandum in Support of his Motion for Leave to File Second Amended Complaint. The proposed pleading is Exhibit A to the Motion. Exhibit B compares Exhibit A against the Complaint (ECF No. 1). Exhibit C compares Exhibit A against the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5). The Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine (“Ballentine Decl.”) accompanies the Motion.

I.	INTRODUCTION

The Court denied Plaintiff’s prior motion for leave (ECF No. 59) for one stated reason: the absence of a redlined comparison. ECF No. 84 at 2. The Order did not find the proposed amendment futile. It did not find prejudice, bad faith, or undue delay. It did not reach the merits of any claim. Meta has said as much: the Court’s orders did not “address the merits of any of Plaintiff’s claims or the arguments raised in Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss,” and nothing in ECF No. 84 “expressly precludes Plaintiff from renewing his request to amend by curing” the omission. ECF No. 101 at 6. NCMEC asked for the chance to respond once a redline was filed. ECF No. 74 at 4. This Motion supplies two comparisons, one against ECF No. 1 and one against ECF No. 5, and presents the request for leave on the complete record.

The proposed Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”) does four things. It names NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, Panayiota Souras, and alleges, on information and belief, that she participated in the approval or authorization described in the First Amended Complaint (“FAC”), which identified among the Doe Defendants “the NCMEC personnel who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 25. It pleads additional facts bearing on falsity, defamatory meaning, and the Defendants’ knowledge. It incorporates events that occurred after August 6, 2026. It keeps the same six counts and the same categories of relief. Leave should be granted under Rules 15(a)(2), 15(d), 20(a)(2), and 21.

II.	BACKGROUND

A.	The Pleadings and the Pending Motions to Dismiss

Plaintiff filed the Complaint on July 30, 2026 (ECF No. 1) and the FAC, as of right, on August 6, 2026 (ECF No. 5). NCMEC moved to dismiss on August 12, 2026 (ECF Nos. 10, 11). Meta moved to dismiss on August 21, 2026 (ECF Nos. 21, 22) and replied on August 31, 2026 (ECF No. 39). Hall moved to dismiss on September 2, 2026, adopting and joining NCMEC’s motion and memorandum (ECF No. 45). No Defendant has answered. No scheduling order has issued. On October 29, 2026, the Court stated that “the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2.

B.	ECF Nos. 59, 64, and 84

On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff moved for leave to file a second amended and supplemental complaint, attaching the complete proposed pleading as Exhibit A (ECF Nos. 59, 59-1, 60). On September 9, 2026, the Court found that it “does not possess sufficient information to issue an Order on this matter” and directed Plaintiff to provide, by September 11, 2026, a redlined version that “must clearly indicate the changes, deletions, and additions that were made to Plaintiff’s Complaint [Dkt. No. 1].” ECF No. 64. NCMEC and Hall opposed ECF No. 59 on September 18, 2026 (ECF No. 74). Meta opposed on September 22, 2026 (ECF No. 83). On October 7, 2026, the Court denied ECF No. 59 on the ground that Plaintiff “was given ample opportunity to comply with the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order [Dkt. No. 64] by producing a redlined Second Amended Complaint but has failed to do so as of the date of this Order.” ECF No. 84 at 2. Plaintiff’s Rule 72(a) objections to ECF Nos. 64 and 84 and related applications remain pending (ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68, 89, 90, 91, 93, 94).

C.	The Proposed Pleading

The SAC is one integrated pleading of 319 numbered paragraphs. It contains a Preliminary Statement, Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, Scope of Allegations, Facts in Sections A through T, six Counts, a Prayer for Relief, and a Demand for Jury Trial. Ex. A.

The SAC adds Souras as a defendant. It alleges that she served as NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer at its Alexandria headquarters; that she was responsible for NCMEC’s legal affairs, including litigation and compliance; that she practiced at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP before joining NCMEC in 2006; that Orrick represented Meta in the two underlying federal actions and received Plaintiff’s April 9, 2026 materials on Meta’s behalf; and that she has performed related functions in prior CyberTipline litigation. Ex. A ¶¶ 21, 91–96. It alleges, on information and belief, that Souras participated in the handling of the April 9, 2026 request, approved the wording of the April 22, 2026 letters, and authorized or directed Hall to issue them before formal service. Ex. A ¶¶ 99–101. It identifies the records, within NCMEC’s control, that would confirm or refute them. Ex. A ¶ 104. It pleads the mental states with which she acted and the purpose her participation served. Ex. A ¶ 102.

The SAC adds facts concerning Plaintiff’s legal name and his Meta accounts, and, on information and belief, the contents of the two CyberTipline reports the letters reference. Ex. A § T; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 3–11. It adds facts concerning the letters’ content defects and the meaning a reasonable reader would take from them. Ex. A §§ K, L. It incorporates events after August 6, 2026: NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum, the August 13, 2026 correspondence with counsel for NCMEC and Hall, Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California, and Hall’s September 2, 2026 filings. Ex. A §§ P, S.

The proposed Second Amended Complaint retains federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1), supplemental jurisdiction under § 1367(a), and restores § 1332(a)(1) as an alternative basis for original jurisdiction over the state-law claims, as supported by the citizenship and amount-in-controversy allegations. Ex. A ¶¶ 9–11.

III.	GOVERNING STANDARDS

A.	Amendment

Rule 15(a)(2) provides that the Court “should freely give leave when justice so requires.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2). Absent “undue delay, bad faith or dilatory motive on the part of the movant, repeated failure to cure deficiencies by amendments previously allowed, undue prejudice to the opposing party by virtue of allowance of the amendment, futility of amendment, etc.,” leave “should, as the rules require, be ‘freely given.’” Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962). The Fourth Circuit reads Rule 15(a) “to provide that ‘leave to amend a pleading should be denied only when the amendment would be prejudicial to the opposing party, there has been bad faith on the part of the moving party, or the amendment would have been futile.’” Laber v. Harvey, 438 F.3d 404, 426 (4th Cir. 2006) (en banc) (quoting Johnson v. Oroweat Foods Co., 785 F.2d 503, 509 (4th Cir. 1986)). “Delay alone, however, is an insufficient reason to deny the plaintiff’s motion to amend.” Id. at 427. “Rather, the delay must be accompanied by prejudice, bad faith, or futility.” Edwards v. City of Goldsboro, 178 F.3d 231, 242 (4th Cir. 1999).

B.	Supplementation

Rule 15(d) permits the Court, “[o]n motion and reasonable notice,” to allow a party, “on just terms,” to serve “a supplemental pleading setting out any transaction, occurrence, or event that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d). “The court may permit supplementation even though the original pleading is defective in stating a claim or defense.” Id. The standards governing amendment and supplementation “are nearly identical. In either situation, leave should be freely granted, and should be denied only where ‘good reason exists . . . , such as prejudice to the defendants.’” Franks v. Ross, 313 F.3d 184, 198 n.15 (4th Cir. 2002) (citation omitted).

C.	Joinder of an Additional Defendant

Rule 20(a)(2) permits persons to be joined as defendants if “any right to relief is asserted against them jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences” and “any question of law or fact common to all defendants will arise in the action.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 20(a)(2). Rule 21 provides that “[o]n motion or on its own, the court may at any time, on just terms, add or drop a party.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 21. Rule 15(a) governs an amendment that adds a party. Galustian v. Peter, 591 F.3d 724, 730 (4th Cir. 2010) (“While some courts have concluded that Rule 15(a) does not apply to amendments seeking to add parties, . . . most courts, including this one, have concluded otherwise.”). A court deciding such a motion “must consider both the general principles of amendment provided by Rule 15(a) and also the more specific joinder provisions of Rule 20(a).” Hinson v. Norwest Fin. S.C., Inc., 239 F.3d 611, 618 (4th Cir. 2001).

D.	Futility

“Futility is apparent if the proposed amended complaint fails to state a claim under the applicable rules and accompanying standards.” Katyle v. Penn Nat’l Gaming, Inc., 637 F.3d 462, 471 (4th Cir. 2011). The applicable standard is Rule 12(b)(6). A complaint satisfies it when it pleads “sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)). The Court accepts the well-pleaded facts as true and draws reasonable inferences in the plaintiff’s favor. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Kolon Indus., Inc., 637 F.3d 435, 440 (4th Cir. 2011). The Court does not adopt a defendant’s characterization of a defendant-authored document as established fact at the pleading stage. Goines v. Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd., 822 F.3d 159, 167–69 (4th Cir. 2016).

IV.	ARGUMENT

A.	The Only Stated Ground for Denying ECF No. 59 Is Eliminated.

ECF No. 64 required a comparison against the Complaint (ECF No. 1). Exhibit B is that comparison. Exhibit C compares the SAC against the operative FAC (ECF No. 5), so that the Court and the Defendants can see exactly what the Motion proposes to change in the pleading now in effect. Exhibit A is the clean copy. Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 14–16.

That submission tracks the form this Court has prescribed for a renewed motion for leave. In Vogel v. RMAC Trust Series 2016-CTT, No. 1:24-cv-2182 (RDA/LRV) (E.D. Va. Apr. 11, 2025), the Court denied a motion for leave without prejudice and stated that if the plaintiffs wished to seek leave again, they “should be allowed to file a renewed motion to amend their Complaint, together with (1) a redlined copy of the proposed amended Complaint against the original Complaint, and (2) a clean copy of the proposed amended Complaint,” with a motion that “set[s] forth sufficient information for the Court to assess whether the Rule 15 standard is met.” Meta cited that order in opposing Plaintiff’s objections. ECF No. 101 at 4–5. This Motion follows it.

ECF No. 84 reached nothing else. It made no finding under Foman or Laber. Meta has told the Court that neither ECF No. 64 nor ECF No. 84 “dismissed any of Plaintiff’s claims nor did they address the merits of any of Plaintiff’s claims or the arguments raised in Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss,” and that “nothing in Magistrate Judge Davis’s order expressly precludes Plaintiff from renewing his request to amend by curing his failure to comply with the Court’s order requiring Plaintiff submit a redlined version of the proposed amended complaint.” ECF No. 101 at 6. NCMEC “request[ed] the opportunity to supplement or amend this Opposition, if and when Plaintiff submits the redline version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint.” ECF No. 74 at 4. The comparison is now before the Court and the Defendants. The Rule 15 question is presented on its merits for the first time.

B.	Rule 15(a)(2) Supplies the Governing Standard.

No scheduling order has issued under Rule 16(b). ECF No. 84 at 1–2; ECF No. 108 at 1–2. The good-cause requirement of Rule 16(b)(4) does not apply. Rule 15(a)(2) alone governs the amendment, and Rule 15(d) governs the supplemental matter under a standard that is “nearly identical.” Franks, 313 F.3d at 198 n.15.

C.	Joinder of Souras Satisfies Rules 20(a)(2) and 21.

Every claim against Souras arises from the same transaction as every claim in the FAC: the preparation, review, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of the two April 22, 2026 letters. Ex. A ¶¶ 10, 21, 91–104, 154, 199. Counts I, II, V, and VI assert rights to relief against Souras jointly and severally with Hall and NCMEC. Count IV asserts a right to relief against her jointly and severally with all Defendants. Ex. A, Prayer for Relief ¶¶ A, C, D, E. The questions common to Souras and the existing Defendants include whether the letters issued before formal service of any subpoena, what meaning a reasonable reader would take from the letters, whether the imputation was false, who within NCMEC’s Office of Legal Counsel reviewed and approved the letters, and whether the issuance fell within the responsibilities and functions described in 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(a). Ex. A §§ I, J, K, L, T. Rule 20(a)(2) is satisfied.

The FAC named among the Doe Defendants “the NCMEC personnel who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters,” stated that their identities “are maintained within the records of . . . NCMEC,” and stated that Plaintiff “will seek leave to amend to identify the Doe Defendants when their identities are ascertained.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 25. As Plaintiff states in his Declaration, the SAC alleges, on information and belief, that Souras participated in the approval or authorization described in ECF No. 5 ¶ 25, and Plaintiff discovered her connection to Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP this past weekend during deeper research. Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 12–13. The SAC names her on that allegation. It does so before any answer, before any scheduling order, and before any discovery. Joinder “on just terms” under Rule 21 requires nothing more.

Subject-matter jurisdiction over the claims against Souras is secure. Count IV, asserted against her, arises under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2). 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1343(a)(1). The state-law claims against her form part of the same case or controversy, and 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) extends supplemental jurisdiction to “claims that involve the joinder or intervention of additional parties.” Ex. A ¶ 10; see Hinson, 239 F.3d at 618.

D.	The Amendment Prejudices No Defendant.

“Whether an amendment is prejudicial will often be determined by the nature of the amendment and its timing.” Laber, 438 F.3d at 427. A prejudicial amendment is one that “raises a new legal theory that would require the gathering and analysis of facts not already considered by the [defendant, and] is offered shortly before or during trial.” Id. (alteration in original) (citation omitted). An amendment “is not prejudicial, by contrast, if it merely adds an additional theory of recovery to the facts already pled and is offered before any discovery has occurred.” Id.

The SAC does less than the amendment Laber describes as non-prejudicial. It adds no theory of recovery. It keeps the same six counts, the same two letters, and the same categories of relief. It is offered before any answer and before any discovery. ECF No. 108 at 2. No discovery has been taken that would have to be reopened. No trial date exists.

The Defendants have already briefed the subjects the SAC addresses: truth and substantial truth, the referent of the letters, privilege, 18 U.S.C. § 2258D, and the sufficiency of the conspiracy allegations. ECF Nos. 11, 22, 39, 45, 74, 83. The contents of the two CyberTipline reports, the internal routing of the April 9, 2026 request, and the approval records for the April 22, 2026 letters are within NCMEC’s records and, to the extent Meta submitted either report, Meta’s records. Ex. A ¶¶ 104, 152, 232. The August 2026 and September 2026 filings pleaded in Section P are Defendants’ own statements. “Because defendant was from the outset made fully aware of the events giving rise to the action, an allowance of the amendment could not in any way prejudice the preparation of the defendant’s case.” Davis v. Piper Aircraft Corp., 615 F.2d 606, 613 (4th Cir. 1980).

Joinder of Souras adds no prejudice to the existing Defendants. NCMEC has been a party since July 31, 2026. ECF No. 3. Souras is alleged to have acted as NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, within NCMEC’s Office of Legal Counsel, on the same letters NCMEC has defended since June 2026. Ex. A ¶¶ 19, 21, 98–101, 157. NCMEC is already sued for her conduct within the scope of her employment. Ex. A ¶ 19. Naming her individually requires no Defendant to gather facts it has not already considered.

NCMEC and Meta argue that the SAC would be a “fifth version of a complaint as to this dispute” and that further amendment would require “a third motion to dismiss.” ECF No. 74 at 1 n.1, 6; ECF No. 83 at 1–2. The Foman factor those arguments invoke is “repeated failure to cure deficiencies by amendments previously allowed.” 371 U.S. at 182. No amendment in this action has been allowed by leave. The FAC was filed as of right under Rule 15(a)(1). ECF No. 5. ECF No. 26 was withdrawn before decision. ECF No. 62. ECF No. 59 was denied on the comparison ground alone. ECF No. 84 at 2. No court has found deficient any pleading Plaintiff has filed concerning the April 22, 2026 letters. The complaint in the 1341 Action was voluntarily dismissed under Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) before any ruling. Ex. A ¶ 174. A defendant’s obligation to respond to an amended pleading under Rule 15(a)(3) is the ordinary consequence of amendment, not the prejudice Laber describes. The motions to dismiss now pending address the same letters, the same claims, and the same defenses the SAC addresses. ECF Nos. 11, 22, 45.

E.	There Is No Bad Faith or Dilatory Motive.

The record reflects the following. The Court denied ECF No. 59 on October 7, 2026. ECF No. 84. Plaintiff files this Motion on November 1, 2026, with the comparison ECF No. 64 described and a second comparison against the operative pleading. The SAC names a defendant alleged, on information and belief, to have participated in the approval or authorization the FAC described in August 2026. ECF No. 5 ¶ 25. It adds no claim. No Defendant has answered. No discovery has begun. Those facts reflect no bad faith and no dilatory motive.

F.	The Amendment Is Not Futile.

Futility turns on whether the SAC states a claim under Rule 12(b)(6). Katyle, 637 F.3d at 471. The Court accepts the well-pleaded facts as true. Kolon, 637 F.3d at 440. The Court need not resolve the pending Rule 12 arguments to find that the SAC is not futile. It need only find that the SAC pleads facts that, accepted as true, state the six claims notwithstanding the defenses asserted.

1.	The claims against Hall, NCMEC, and Meta.

The SAC pleads facts addressed to each dismissal theory the Defendants have asserted. ECF Nos. 11, 22, 39, 45.

First, the SAC distinguishes an advance notice of intended subpoenas from formally served compulsory process. The April 9, 2026 transmission was captioned “Advance Notice of Intended Subpoenas — Two Separate Matters,” enclosed signed subpoenas, and stated that formal service would occur after the notice period had run. Neither subpoena was served. No return, proof of service, or court order existed. Plaintiff neither waived service nor requested an early response. Ex. A §§ G, I (¶¶ 54–56, 72–75).

Second, the SAC pleads the voluntary and private issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters. The letters were addressed to Plaintiff alone, were not copied to any court or counsel, and were not filed in either action. They were not CyberTipline reports or referrals and were not undertaken as part of any effort to identify a child victim. Ex. A ¶¶ 79–80. The SAC pleads that the conduct was intentional, was undertaken with actual malice and reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury without legal justification, and served the litigation-directed purpose alleged in Section Q. Ex. A ¶ 80.

Third, the SAC pleads source-level falsity. Plaintiff’s legal name is Marvelle J. Ballentine. Before April 22, 2026, he never used that name to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any Meta account. The Facebook account associated with the July 4, 2022 enforcement event was maintained under the name “Jay Ballentine.” On information and belief, neither report referenced in the letters, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” and neither concerned Plaintiff personally. Ex. A § T; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 3–11.

Fourth, the SAC pleads person-level falsity and defamatory implication. The letters placed Plaintiff’s full legal name in the same sentence as “two CyberTipline reports,” joined Plaintiff’s three search identifiers disjunctively in the order he supplied them, identified no report number, date, provider, or matched identifier, and omitted every limiting statement. Ex. A §§ K, L (¶¶ 105–119). The SAC pleads the meaning a reasonable reader would take from the letters. Ex. A ¶¶ 117, 194.

Fifth, the SAC pleads facts supporting Hall’s knowledge, intent, recklessness, and actual malice as of April 22, 2026: her access to NCMEC’s legal-intake records showing no service; her selection of language characterizing the letters as responses to a subpoena; her disjunctive listing of Plaintiff’s own search terms without disambiguation; and her omission of every source-identifying detail. Ex. A §§ I, K, T; Ex. A ¶¶ 244–246. The later events in Section P are pleaded as bearing on subsequent knowledge, continuing position, the unresolved referent of the letters, and continuing injury, not as proof of what Hall knew on April 22, 2026. Ex. A ¶¶ 173, 185, 188, 289.

Sixth, the SAC pleads Plaintiff’s disclosed survivor status and Hall’s knowledge of it before April 22, 2026. Ex. A §§ C, G (¶¶ 39–45, 60); Ex. A ¶ 283.

Seventh, the SAC pleads the circumstantial facts supporting the alleged agreement: identical materials to NCMEC and to counsel for Meta and Accenture on April 9, 2026; motions on April 21, 2026 directed at the same discovery; imminent depositions; no formal service and no court order requiring a response; two case-keyed letters one day after those motions; issuance before the notice period expired; omission of every source-identifying detail; an unsworn assertion, outside the discovery process, on the subject scheduled for sworn examination; and issuance while the motions remained pending. Ex. A § O (¶¶ 141–151).

Eighth, the SAC pleads the object of the understanding and the deterrence directed at Plaintiff’s attendance as a party and his testimony as a prospective witness. Ex. A § Q (¶¶ 190–196).

Ninth, the SAC pleads overt acts by each Defendant and personal injury with physical manifestation, impaired capacity, and litigation-related consequences. Ex. A §§ R, S (¶¶ 197–213).

Meta’s opposition to ECF No. 59 argued that the allegation concerning Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California “has no relevance whatsoever to Plaintiff’s claims against Meta.” ECF No. 83 at 3. The SAC pleads that filing only as a subsequent fact bearing on Meta’s knowledge, state of mind, and awareness of the relationship between the two proceedings. Ex. A ¶¶ 185, 297. It states that no claim rests on the filing and that liability under Count IV rests on Sections O, Q, and R. Ex. A ¶ 297. The weight of one subsequent-knowledge allegation does not determine whether Count IV states a claim. Count IV rests on the agreement alleged in Section O, the purpose alleged in Section Q, the overt acts alleged in Section R, and the injury alleged in Section S. Ex. A ¶¶ 290–299.

2.	The claims against Souras.

The SAC pleads each element of each count against Souras. For Counts I and II, it pleads her participation in publication by approving the wording and authorizing or directing issuance (Ex. A ¶¶ 235, 259); falsity (¶¶ 242–243, 266–267); negligence and, separately, actual malice, with the facts from which each is inferred (¶¶ 247, 271); and scope of employment (¶¶ 249, 273). For Count IV, it pleads her knowing participation in implementing the agreement, her knowledge of the pending actions and the announced formal service, her sharing of the purpose, and her overt acts (¶¶ 102, 154, 199, 294, 296). For Count V, it pleads her part in the combination and its execution (¶¶ 302–303). For Count VI, it pleads her approval of the words communicated to Plaintiff and her knowledge or reckless disregard of their falsity (¶¶ 311, 316).

NCMEC has invoked 18 U.S.C. § 2258D. ECF No. 11 at 7. That section bars civil claims “against NCMEC, including any director, officer, employee, or agent of NCMEC, arising from the performance of the CyberTipline responsibilities or functions of NCMEC.” 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(a). It does not apply where the officer or employee “engaged in intentional misconduct,” acted “with actual malice,” acted “with reckless disregard to a substantial risk of causing injury without legal justification,” or acted “for a purpose unrelated to the performance of any responsibility or function under this section, section 2258A or 2258C of this title, or section 404 of the Missing Children’s Assistance Act (34 U.S.C. 11293).” 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(b). The SAC pleads, as to Souras, that her review, approval, and authorization “were not part of any effort to identify a child victim,” and that her participation “was intentional, was undertaken with actual malice and reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury without legal justification, and served the litigation-directed purpose alleged in Section Q.” Ex. A ¶ 102. Those allegations track subsection (b). The SAC attaches the facts from which they are inferred: the letters were voluntary correspondence, issued before formal service, without any court order, addressed to Plaintiff alone, keyed to two pending federal actions in which the recipient’s own counsel had moved to stay the same discovery one day earlier. Ex. A §§ G, H, I, J, O. Whether the exception applies is a merits question. At the pleading stage the question is whether the SAC pleads facts that, taken as true, fall within subsection (b). It does.

The allegations of Souras’s participation are pleaded on information and belief, and the SAC says so in each instance. The Fourth Circuit has held that factual “allegations pled on information and belief are not categorically insufficient to state a claim for relief where the proof supporting the allegation is within the sole possession and control of the defendant or where the belief is based on sufficient factual material that makes the inference of culpability plausible.” Lowy v. Daniel Defense, LLC, No. 24-1822, slip op. at 34–35 (4th Cir. Feb. 11, 2026) (citation omitted). Such allegations “may not be wholly conclusory,” and must be “supported by . . . well-pled facts that exist independent of [the plaintiff’s] legal conclusions.” Kashdan v. George Mason Univ., 70 F.4th 694, 701 (4th Cir. 2023). The SAC satisfies both conditions. It pleads the facts on which the belief rests: Souras’s responsibility for NCMEC’s litigation and compliance matters; her documented performance of related functions in CyberTipline litigation; her former employment at Orrick, which represented Meta in both actions and received the April 9, 2026 materials for Meta; the arrival of the request at NCMEC’s Legal Department; the issuance of the response by Hall, as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel, on NCMEC letterhead in two pending federal actions; and the chronology in Sections G through I. Ex. A ¶¶ 91–98; Ex. A §§ G–I. It states that the identities of other reviewers, the internal routing, the communications, and any approval records are maintained in NCMEC’s records and cannot be reached without discovery. Ex. A ¶ 104. Those are well-pleaded facts independent of the legal conclusion. The inference that NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer reviewed and approved case-captioned legal correspondence issued by her office in two pending federal actions is plausible on those facts.

3.	The futility arguments already made do not establish futility.

NCMEC argued that “[n]o allegations Plaintiff can make can change” the asserted truth of the letters “because he does not have access to those reports.” ECF No. 74 at 5. That argument asks the Court to treat NCMEC’s characterization of its own letters as established fact. At the pleading stage the Court does not do so. Goines, 822 F.3d at 167–69. The SAC pleads, with the factual basis, that neither report as received identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine” and that neither concerned Plaintiff personally. Ex. A ¶¶ 228–232. It pleads that NCMEC’s own memorandum framed the referent as Plaintiff, “a person with the same name,” or an e-mail address, and that counsel declined to answer which identifier, if any, appears in either report. Ex. A ¶¶ 176, 178–179, 215. Those allegations are accepted as true on a futility inquiry. Kolon, 637 F.3d at 440.

NCMEC also argued that the amendment is “unnecessary” because Plaintiff could present the same points in opposition briefs. ECF No. 74 at 5–6. A plaintiff’s ability to argue a point in a brief does not bear on whether the proposed pleading states a claim, which is the futility question. Katyle, 637 F.3d at 471. Facts belong in the pleading. The SAC places them there.

G.	Rule 15(d) Supports Incorporating the Subsequent Events into One Operative Pleading.

Section P pleads events after August 6, 2026: NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum stating that NCMEC “responded to the subpoenas without awaiting formal service” and that the linkage may involve “a person with the same name”; Plaintiff’s August 13, 2026 question to counsel and counsel’s response; Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California citing this action; and Hall’s September 2, 2026 filings adopting NCMEC’s positions. Ex. A ¶¶ 175–189. Count III pleads that the severe emotional distress on which it rests continued after the FAC was filed while the referent of the letters remained unresolved. Ex. A ¶ 289. Each is a “transaction, occurrence, or event that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d). Each concerns the same letters, the same Defendants, and the same claims. Each bears on knowledge, state of mind, the referent of the letters, or continuing injury. The Scope of Allegations limits their use: court filings are pleaded “solely as facts establishing timing, notice, knowledge, coordination, and admissions,” and “[n]one is conduct on which any claim rests.” Ex. A ¶ 25.

One integrated pleading serves efficient adjudication. Defendants respond to one pleading. The Court adjudicates one set of allegations. Rule 15(d) exists to permit that result, and the Fourth Circuit treats a pleading that both amends and supplements under the same standard. Franks, 313 F.3d at 198 n.15.

H.	Procedural Effect of Granting Leave.

Granting leave has the following consequences. First, the SAC supersedes the FAC. “[A]n amended pleading ordinarily supersedes the original and renders it of no legal effect.” Young v. City of Mount Ranier, 238 F.3d 567, 572 (4th Cir. 2001) (citation omitted). Second, Defendants Hall, NCMEC, and Meta respond within the time provided by Rule 15(a)(3) or such other time as the Court directs. Third, the Clerk issues a summons for Souras under Rule 4(b), and Plaintiff serves her under Rule 4.

Plaintiff’s pending objections and applications concerning ECF Nos. 64 and 84 remain submitted in their respective proceedings. Granting this Motion would provide the immediate relief of permitting the proposed superseding pleading. Plaintiff requests no determination through this Motion concerning the continued justiciability or disposition of the remaining objections or retrospective-relief requests, which remain subject to the effect of any relief actually granted.

The pending motions to dismiss directed to the FAC (ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45) are procedural context. This Motion requests no disposition of them. Their management after the SAC becomes the operative pleading remains within the Court’s discretion. NCMEC’s alternative request that leave be held in abeyance until the motions to dismiss are decided (ECF No. 74 at 7) would have the Court adjudicate a pleading the SAC replaces. Rule 15(d) permits supplementation “even though the original pleading is defective in stating a claim or defense.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d). Deciding leave first permits the Court to adjudicate one complete pleading once.
